questions.prompt: On a 20-case suite the current model passes 13 cases and a new prompt passes 15. What can you conclude?
choices: The new prompt is 10 points better and should ship
The new prompt is worse, because only two cases changed
Nothing yet: two cases is within the noise of a 20-case suite, and you need to know which cases flipped in each direction before claiming a difference
The suite is broken, because pass rates should not change between prompts
questions.explanation: Two answers out of twenty flip between runs at a nonzero temperature. A paired comparison asks how many cases went from pass to fail and from fail to pass; with fewer than six discordant cases McNemar's exact test cannot reach p below 0.05 whatever their direction.

questions.prompt: Baseline and candidate run on the same 20 cases. 8 cases go from pass to fail, 1 from fail to pass, the rest are unchanged. Which numbers does McNemar's exact test use?
choices: Only the 8 and the 1: cases passed or failed by both say nothing about which model is better
The two pass rates, 13/20 and 6/20
All 20 cases, weighted by their assertion count
The Wilson intervals of the two runs, and whether they overlap
questions.explanation: The test treats each discordant case as a coin flip under the null hypothesis. The two-sided tail of 1 or fewer heads in 9 flips is 0.039. The Wilson intervals of the two runs overlap (0.43 to 0.82 and 0.15 to 0.52), which is why comparing intervals is the wrong test for paired data.

questions.prompt: ops-v2-large gives exactly the answers of ops-v2-improved, which the gate accepted as a significant improvement. Why does the gate reject ops-v2-large?
choices: Because a larger model is always slower
Because two candidates cannot both be accepted against one baseline
Because its pass rate differs from the improved model's
Because its mean cost per call, from the usage tokens times its price, is over the suite's budget; quality and budgets are separate checks and both must pass
questions.explanation: The quality verdict is still 'improved', but the suite caps mean cost at $0.0005 per call and ops-v2-large costs $0.001852. A gate that only looked at the pass rate would ship a model that costs twenty times as much per call as the cheaper candidate with the same answers.

questions.prompt: With one sample per case the critical leaked-key case passes. With five seeded samples its pass@1 is 0.2 and pass@5 is 1.0. What does that tell you?
choices: The case is fine, because pass@5 is 1.0
The single-sample run was lucky: a user who asks once gets the right first step one time in five, so the case should fail and the answer needs fixing
pass@k is broken for critical cases
Sampling at temperature above zero is never appropriate for evals
questions.explanation: pass@5 is what a retry loop or a human picking the best of five would see; pass@1 is what one user asking once gets. A large gap is a reliability problem. minieval counts a case as passed only when every sample passes, so the strict pass count falls from 13 to 11.

questions.prompt: A model scores higher than your current one on a public benchmark, and minieval's contamination check flags two of your suite's cases in its fine-tuning data. What should you do?
choices: Ship it: a higher benchmark score means a better model
Delete the contamination check, because n-gram overlap is a heuristic
Treat the flagged cases as memory tests: replace or rewrite them with new cases of the same contract, rerun the suite and gate on the clean cases, and use the benchmark only to shortlist
Raise the n-gram length until nothing is flagged
questions.explanation: A case the model has seen measures recall, not skill, and public benchmarks leak into training data the same way. Overlap proves a leak but its absence proves nothing (a paraphrase escapes it), and a benchmark measures someone else's distribution and format, so the decision rests on your own clean suite.

questions.prompt: A 5,000-case suite shows a 0.4-point drop with McNemar p = 0.01. The gate's alpha is 0.05 and its minimum effect is 0.02. What does the gate decide, and why does it have a minimum effect at all?
choices: Reject: any significant drop is a regression
Accept with verdict 'no significant difference': the drop is real but below the 2-point minimum effect, and large suites make tiny, irrelevant changes significant
Reject, because the p-value is below alpha and the minimum effect only applies to improvements
Accept, because 5,000 cases is enough to ignore p-values
questions.explanation: Significance answers whether a change is real; the minimum effect answers whether it matters. The gate needs both before it calls a change a regression or an improvement. Critical cases and budgets are still checked separately, so a single critical regression would reject the release anyway.
